_comment: Mini-game question banks for g1 (Plan Your Week) and g2 (Nutrition / Menu Challenge). Grown from the small inline bank previously in server.py to 15-20 questions each, drawn from the three curriculum areas (Planning for Healthy Eating, Applying Nutrition Information, Assembling Balanced Meals). Rounds group related scenarios so the game feels like levels; each choice carries a one-line explanation for instant feedback. New items added in this pass are marked 'draft': true so the nutrition team can review before they go live; items without that flag were already approved copy from the original bank. g3 is the plate builder — its logic stays in plate_composer; scoring criteria are intentionally NOT invented here (see server.py plate scoring TODO).

games.title: Plan Your Week
games.intro: A busy week ahead with a tight budget. Make choices that set you up to eat well.

scenarios.prompt: It's Sunday. You have 30 minutes and $40 for groceries. What's your move?

choices.text: Buy flexible staples: beans, oats, frozen veg, eggs
choices.feedback: Flexible, affordable staples make weekday meals effortless.

choices.text: Skip the store, you'll figure it out daily
choices.feedback: No plan often means last-minute takeout. A few staples remove that pressure.

choices.text: Spend it all on one fancy dinner
choices.feedback: Fun, but it leaves the rest of the week unplanned and over budget.

scenarios.prompt: You have 60 minutes to meal-prep. Pick the highest-return task.

choices.text: Cook a big pot of grains and roast a tray of veg
choices.feedback: Two bases cover 5-6 lunches with light assembly later.

choices.text: Pre-slice fruit for the whole week
choices.feedback: Nice touch, but fruit on its own doesn't carry lunches — bases do.

choices.text: Make one elaborate dinner for tonight
choices.feedback: Weeknight-you will thank weekend-you more for bases than for a single feast.

scenarios.prompt: Your pantry has beans, rice, canned tomatoes, oats, and frozen spinach. Lean protein from the fridge: eggs. What's a plan-friendly default lunch?

choices.text: Rice + beans + spinach bowl with a fried egg on top
choices.feedback: Whole grain, a protein source, and a vegetable — classic flexible balance.

choices.text: Buttered toast and coffee
choices.feedback: Light on protein and vegetables — it won't carry you to dinner.

choices.text: Order delivery because the pantry's 'boring'
choices.feedback: Those pantry staples ARE the plan — they're how balanced eating survives a busy week.

scenarios.prompt: Grocery store, $25 left and a cart with chicken and rice. One more pick to round out the week.

choices.text: A bag of frozen broccoli + a bag of apples
choices.feedback: Produce you won't lose to spoilage, and a snack-ready fruit — strong finish.

choices.text: A tub of ice cream
choices.feedback: Not a sin, but it doesn't earn the slot — a vegetable or fruit would carry more meals.

choices.text: An energy drink 12-pack
choices.feedback: Expensive, high in added sugar, and doesn't build any meal.

scenarios.prompt: You're planning the week on paper. What's the most useful first line?

choices.text: List the 3 nights you'll actually be home to cook
choices.feedback: Anchor the plan to your real schedule — then meals get built around it.

choices.text: Write out seven unique dinner recipes
choices.feedback: Ambitious, but a plan that assumes you cook every night usually breaks.

choices.text: Just copy last week's plan
choices.feedback: If last week worked — fair! If it didn't, same list = same problem.

scenarios.prompt: Wednesday is packed. How do you handle lunch?

choices.text: Batch-prepped grain bowl from Sunday
choices.feedback: Prepping ahead pays off exactly on days like this.

choices.text: Skip lunch to save time
choices.feedback: Skipping tends to backfire later. A quick prepped option keeps you steady.

choices.text: Grab a candy bar from a vending machine
choices.feedback: Fast, but mostly added sugar — it won't carry you to dinner.

scenarios.prompt: You wake up late. What's the realistic breakfast move?

choices.text: Yogurt + fruit grabbed on the way out
choices.feedback: Protein + fruit, zero prep — the point of a plan is to make this easy.

choices.text: Nothing — you'll 'catch up' later
choices.feedback: Catching up usually becomes grazing on whatever's handy, not a balanced meal.

choices.text: A large sweetened coffee drink
choices.feedback: Mostly added sugar — hunger and energy will crash by late morning.

scenarios.prompt: It's 9 PM, you're home, you haven't eaten dinner. Pantry only.

choices.text: Tuna + whole-wheat crackers + a side of frozen veg microwaved
choices.feedback: Protein, whole grain, vegetable — a balanced plate in six minutes.

choices.text: Bowl of sugary cereal with milk
choices.feedback: Quick, but mostly refined carbs and added sugar before bed.

choices.text: Skip dinner, go to bed
choices.feedback: Skipping dinner often means stronger late-night cravings or a rougher sleep.

scenarios.prompt: Friends invite you out for dinner, but you'd planned to cook. What's the plan-flexible move?

choices.text: Go out, swap tonight's planned meal to tomorrow
choices.feedback: A plan is a guide, not a cage. Shift it and go.

choices.text: Say no and eat your sad planned pasta alone
choices.feedback: Social meals matter — rigid plans tend to collapse under this exact pressure.

choices.text: Order DoorDash on top of the planned ingredients
choices.feedback: Double food, double cost — the ingredients spoil instead of getting used.

scenarios.prompt: You open the fridge Thursday night. The planned chicken is a day past its 'use by' and smells off.

choices.text: Toss it, assemble a pantry stir-fry with beans and frozen veg
choices.feedback: Spoiled protein is a hard no — pantry staples exist for exactly this moment.

choices.text: Cook it anyway, it 'should' be fine
choices.feedback: Not worth the food-poisoning risk — trust the pantry backup instead.

choices.text: Skip dinner and go to bed hungry
choices.feedback: Fallback eating is what pantry staples are for — a plan isn't 'ruined' by swapping proteins.

scenarios.prompt: Three cheapest-per-serving protein sources in a typical US grocery store?

choices.text: Dried beans, eggs, canned tuna
choices.feedback: All three come in well under $1 per serving most weeks.

choices.text: Shrimp, steak, salmon fillet
choices.feedback: Great foods, but typically the highest-per-serving proteins in the aisle.

choices.text: Protein bars, jerky, protein powder
choices.feedback: Convenient, but priced for the processing — not a per-serving win.

scenarios.prompt: Frozen vegetables vs. fresh — which pick usually wins on a tight budget?

choices.text: Frozen, because nothing wilts before you cook it
choices.feedback: Frozen is nutritionally comparable and dramatically cuts spoilage waste.

choices.text: Fresh — frozen 'isn't real food'
choices.feedback: Frozen is just vegetables, picked at peak and flash-frozen. Food is food.

choices.text: Neither — just skip vegetables this week
choices.feedback: A week without vegetables isn't a budget win, it's a nutrition gap.

scenarios.prompt: Store brands vs. name brands on pantry staples (rice, beans, oats)?

choices.text: Store brand — the ingredient is identical
choices.feedback: On commodities like rice and beans, store brand is the same food at 20–40% off.

choices.text: Name brand always — it's higher quality
choices.feedback: True for very few staples. For plain grains and beans, you're paying for marketing.

choices.text: Mix of imported organic specialty items
choices.feedback: Fine occasionally — bad default for a tight budget.

scenarios.prompt: A big-batch pot of chili will stretch across the week. Smartest companion to prep alongside it?

choices.text: A pot of brown rice and a tray of roasted veg
choices.feedback: Rotate the chili over the same two bases to keep lunches from feeling repetitive.

choices.text: A second pot of chili
choices.feedback: You'll be sick of chili by Wednesday — variety sustains the plan.

choices.text: A sheet of brownies
choices.feedback: Treats are fine; they're not the base you're building the week on.

scenarios.prompt: Your campus has a free weekly produce pantry (real on many US campuses). You can take 5 items.

choices.text: Onions, carrots, apples, sweet potatoes, bananas — all keep well
choices.feedback: High-storage-life produce that stretches across many meals — strongest free-food return.

choices.text: Five bags of pre-cut salad
choices.feedback: Pre-cut greens wilt in 2–3 days — most of it will go to waste.

choices.text: Nothing — 'free food is embarrassing'
choices.feedback: Campus produce pantries exist because they help. Taking what you'll eat is exactly the point.

games.title: Nutrition / Menu Challenge
games.intro: Read real labels and menus, and choose with confidence.
games._hidden_notice: DISABLED 2026-10-29 — nutrition team flagged this activity as having inaccurate information and being the wrong Week 2 activity. The Week 2 workflow (backend/content/weeks/week2.json) is the correct Week 2 activity. Visibility is gated by MENU_CHALLENGE_ENABLED=false in server.py. The rounds below are kept for reference only; they are not served to any account.

_pending_rework_slot.note: Nutrition team sample questions go here when they land. Paste the new scenarios + choices under 'rounds'. Keep the schema identical to the other games so no code changes are needed. Set _hidden_notice to null when the activity is reinstated.

scenarios.prompt: Two cereals. A lists sugar as the second ingredient. B lists whole oats as the first ingredient. Which is the whole-grain pick?

choices.text: Cereal B — a whole grain is listed first
choices.feedback: Ingredients are listed in order by weight — first ingredient wins.

choices.text: Cereal A — the front says 'multigrain' so it must count
choices.feedback: 'Multigrain' only means multiple grains; most of them could be refined.

scenarios.prompt: A bread label says 'multigrain' on the front. Where does 'whole grain' actually need to appear to count as a whole-grain product?

choices.text: First on the ingredients list — 'whole wheat flour' or similar
choices.feedback: The front of the pack isn't regulated like the ingredient list. First ingredient wins.

choices.text: Anywhere on the front of the package
choices.feedback: 'Multigrain' only means multiple grains — most of them could be refined.

choices.text: In the brand name
choices.feedback: Brand names aren't regulated — check the first ingredient.

scenarios.prompt: A chip bag says 'serving size: about 15 chips' and 'servings per container: 3.5'. You eat the whole bag. How many servings is that?

choices.text: About 3.5 servings — the whole bag is the total portion
choices.feedback: Servings-per-container scales the whole label — a common place labels understate what you'll actually eat.

choices.text: One serving — the label is for the whole bag
choices.feedback: The nutrition panel is per serving, not per bag. Always check servings-per-container.

choices.text: No way to tell
choices.feedback: You can — multiply the per-serving portion by servings-per-container.

scenarios.prompt: A yogurt label says '0% fat' on the front. The ingredients list sugar as the second ingredient. Fair pick for a low-added-sugar day?

choices.text: No — fat-free yogurts often add sugar to compensate on taste
choices.feedback: Check 'Added Sugars' on the facts panel — fat-free doesn't mean low-sugar.

choices.text: Yes — 0% fat is automatically healthier
choices.feedback: A classic label trap: fat-free products often lead on added sugar.

choices.text: Yes — yogurt is always a safe pick
choices.feedback: Plain yogurt is — sweetened versions often list sugar near the top of the ingredient list.

scenarios.prompt: On a frozen meal, which quick label check is the clearest 'is this high in sodium?' signal?

choices.text: Sodium %DV — anything 20% or higher is 'high' per the FDA
choices.feedback: %DV is the fastest shortcut for 'is this a lot or a little?' — 20%+ is high.

choices.text: The total fat line
choices.feedback: Fat isn't the sodium story — look at the sodium line itself, in %DV.

choices.text: The brand's health claim on the front
choices.feedback: Front-of-pack claims aren't regulated like the facts panel — check sodium %DV instead.

scenarios.prompt: At a burger spot, what's a balanced order?

choices.text: Grilled sandwich, side salad, water
choices.feedback: A balanced build even at a fast-food menu — nicely done.

choices.text: Double patty, large fries, large soda
choices.feedback: Heavy on sodium and low on vegetables. A side swap balances it out.

scenarios.prompt: You're at a Mexican fast-casual chain. What's a balanced build?

choices.text: Burrito bowl: brown rice, black beans, chicken, salsa, lots of veg
choices.feedback: Whole grain + protein + loads of vegetables — a strong build at any chain.

choices.text: Nachos with queso, no sides
choices.feedback: Heavy on refined grains and cheese sauce, almost no vegetables.

choices.text: Three crunchy tacos with meat and cheese only
choices.feedback: Protein + grain, missing the vegetable half of the plate.

scenarios.prompt: Coffee shop stop. You want it to count as breakfast, not a dessert.

choices.text: Oat-milk latte + a protein-and-egg wrap
choices.feedback: Protein + whole grain + liquid — real breakfast, not a sugar bomb.

choices.text: A large sweetened frappé and a muffin
choices.feedback: Mostly added sugar before noon — this is a dessert, not a breakfast.

choices.text: Black coffee and nothing else
choices.feedback: Fine for a caffeine fix, but it's not a meal — hunger will catch up by late morning.

scenarios.prompt: Pizza night with friends. Minimum-regret order style?

choices.text: Thin crust, half veggie, a side salad to share
choices.feedback: Thinner crust + vegetables on top shifts the balance without saying 'no' to pizza.

choices.text: Deep-dish stuffed with pepperoni and sausage
choices.feedback: Heavy on refined grains, cheese and processed meats — occasional is fine, but it's the heaviest option.

choices.text: Skip and sulk about not eating
choices.feedback: Food is part of being with people — a vegetable-heavy slice fits a balanced week fine.

scenarios.prompt: On a drive-thru menu, which drink choice swings the whole order's added-sugar budget?

choices.text: The 32-oz regular soda
choices.feedback: A single large regular soda can carry more added sugar than the entire food side.

choices.text: The side salad
choices.feedback: Salads aren't your added-sugar risk — drinks almost always are.

choices.text: The small coffee, black
choices.feedback: Black coffee adds roughly zero sugar — unless you sweeten it later.

scenarios.prompt: Craving crunch and salt. Lower-sodium swap for a regular bag of chips?

choices.text: Air-popped popcorn with a little olive oil
choices.feedback: Whole grain, low sodium when you salt it yourself, surprisingly satisfying crunch.

choices.text: Pretzels
choices.feedback: Pretzels are actually among the saltier chip-aisle swaps — check the label.

choices.text: Buttery crackers
choices.feedback: Refined grain + butter + salt — not really a swap, just a side-step.

scenarios.prompt: Craving dessert. Lower-added-sugar swap that still tastes like a treat?

choices.text: Plain Greek yogurt + berries + a tiny drizzle of honey
choices.feedback: Protein + fruit, with sweetness you control — fraction of the added sugar of ice cream.

choices.text: A 'diet' soda
choices.feedback: Addresses the sugar hit, but there's no treat and no food — fine occasionally, not a swap.

choices.text: Fruit juice in a wine glass
choices.feedback: Juice is still mostly sugar — about as much as the treat you're swapping.

scenarios.prompt: Which pair of pantry staples swaps in the most added nutrition for the least extra work?

choices.text: Whole-wheat pasta instead of white pasta; brown rice instead of white rice
choices.feedback: Same cook, same meals — just more fiber and more lasting fullness.

choices.text: Flavoured instant ramen instead of plain rice
choices.feedback: Flavoured ramen packets are the sodium champions of the pantry. Big step the wrong way.

choices.text: Cereal bars instead of oatmeal
choices.feedback: Plain oats beat most cereal bars on fiber and added sugar — the bars just look faster.

scenarios.prompt: Store deli: ham vs. turkey vs. roast chicken, all 'oven roasted'. Lowest-sodium pick, usually?

choices.text: Oven-roasted chicken breast, 'low sodium' variant if available
choices.feedback: Chicken breast is usually the lightest-sodium deli meat — doubly so in low-sodium versions.

choices.text: Ham
choices.feedback: Ham is almost always the highest-sodium deli choice — cured meats carry a lot of salt.

choices.text: Flavoured bologna
choices.feedback: Processed luncheon meats run very high in sodium — this is the heaviest, not the lightest.

scenarios.prompt: You take two 'add vegetable' habits for the next week. Which pair gives the highest actual-eaten lift?

choices.text: Keep washed baby carrots at eye level; add frozen spinach to any hot bowl
choices.feedback: Low-friction defaults beat willpower — this is how 'eat more vegetables' actually happens.

choices.text: Buy a specialty vegetable you've never cooked before
choices.feedback: Novel foods usually spoil before they're cooked — great occasionally, poor as a weekly default.

choices.text: Promise to make a huge salad every single night
choices.feedback: Big-promise habits break on busy nights — small, lazy defaults survive.

games.title: Build a Balanced Meal
games.intro: Drag ingredients onto your plate and build a balanced meal, round by round.

daily_challenges._comment: The daily challenge rotates by date (same for every participant on the same day) — chosen deterministically from this pool by index = (date_hash % len). Each awards a fixed 5 points on first correct answer that day.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: comparing two cereals, what's the quickest 'heart-friendly' shortcut on the box?

choices.text: First ingredient is a whole grain, and sugar isn't near the top of the list
choices.feedback: Ingredients are listed in order by weight — a whole grain first, with sugar well down the list, is the hard-to-game shortcut.

choices.text: Zero sugar at all costs
choices.feedback: Not realistic for most pantries — a whole-grain first ingredient matters more than hitting zero.

choices.text: The front of the box says 'heart healthy'
choices.feedback: Front-of-pack claims aren't regulated like the ingredient list — check the ingredients instead.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: a chip bag says 'about 3 servings per container'. You eat the whole bag. How many servings is that?

choices.text: About 3 servings — the whole bag is the total portion
choices.feedback: Servings-per-container scales the whole label — easy label trap once you see it.

choices.text: One serving — the label is for the whole bag
choices.feedback: That's per serving, not per bag — a common portion-size misread.

choices.text: No way to know
choices.feedback: You can — multiply the per-serving portion by servings-per-container.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: the balanced-plate rule of thumb is roughly...

choices.text: Half the plate vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grain, a quarter protein
choices.feedback: Flexible, not rigid — a plate that fits most meals without weighing anything.

choices.text: All protein, no grains at all
choices.feedback: Whole grains are part of a balanced plate — not something to zero out.

choices.text: Mostly grains, a side of vegetables
choices.feedback: Vegetables usually belong on the biggest half of the plate.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: lowest-friction swap to add fiber this week?

choices.text: Swap white rice for brown rice in your usual meals
choices.feedback: Same cook, same meals — just more fiber. The swap is the whole trick.

choices.text: Buy an unfamiliar grain you've never cooked
choices.feedback: Novelty foods often spoil before they're cooked. Great occasionally — not the default lift.

choices.text: Eat only salad for a week
choices.feedback: Not sustainable — small defaults beat heroic promises.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: on a nutrition label, which %DV sodium number does the FDA call 'high'?

choices.text: 20% DV or more
choices.feedback: 20%+ DV = high; 5% or less = low. A clean shortcut for the sodium check.

choices.text: 5% DV
choices.feedback: 5% is low, not high — easy to flip around in your head.

choices.text: Any amount at all
choices.feedback: Sodium is a nutrient you need some of — the rule is 'high', not 'any'.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: realistic breakfast on a late-waking morning?

choices.text: Yogurt and fruit grabbed on the way out
choices.feedback: Protein + fruit, no prep. Low-friction defaults beat 'skip and catch up'.

choices.text: Skip it, catch up with vending-machine chips later
choices.feedback: 'Catching up' usually becomes grazing on whatever's handy — not a balanced plate.

choices.text: Large sweetened coffee drink only
choices.feedback: Mostly added sugar — the crash in two hours isn't worth it.

pool.prompt: Daily challenge: on a tight budget, frozen vegetables vs. fresh?

choices.text: Frozen — comparable nutrition, no spoilage pressure
choices.feedback: Fresh wilts; frozen waits. On a tight budget, frozen wins the week.

choices.text: Fresh — 'frozen isn't real food'
choices.feedback: Frozen is just vegetables picked at peak and flash-frozen. Food is food.

choices.text: Neither, skip vegetables
choices.feedback: Not a budget win — a nutrition gap.
